text.p: Spain's High Court convicted disgraced former Banesto bank chairman Mario Conde of fraud and sentenced him to six years in prison on Thursday in the first verdict arising from the country's biggest financial scandal.

Conde was also ordered to pay more than $5.0 million in the first in a series of trials on charges the former banking magnate and his closest associates committed massive fraud that led to the 1993 collapse of Banco Espanol de Credito-Banesto.
"We convict Mario Conde for the crime of misappropriation of funds and falsifying public documentation on penalty of six years in prison..." Magistrate Ventura Perez said.
Conde will be tried later this year on related charges that carry even stiffer prison sentences.

The case that was decided on Thursday centred on a 600 million peseta payment made in 1990 by Banesto to Argentia Trust, a shadowy company based on the Lesser Antilles island of St. Vincent, a popular tax haven.
Conde was ordered to pay Banesto back the 600 million pesetas ($5.0 million) and was also fined $70,000. When the sentence was handed down, Conde was free on bail.
Conde said in his defence that the payment went to a well-connected intermediary, Antonio Navalon, who helped Banesto get approval from Spain's former Socialist government for some business deals.
He denied he had ever asked Navalon to make payments to anyone in the government or in the Socialist party.

The court alleged Conde and his associates were responsible for Banesto's collapse because they hid the true financial state of the bank, which had run up a deficit in 1993 of 605 billion pesetas ($5.5 billion) in 1993.
The most serious case involving Banesto, in which Conde is accused of siphoning off large sums from the bank's accounts for his personal use, is not expected to start before October.
If convicted on those charges, he could face 35 to 44 years in prison. But the case could drag on for years.
Conde headed Banesto for six years before the Bank of Spain stepped in and removed the board.

A little-known lawyer before he bought his way onto the Banesto board in 1987, Conde's flair for business elevated him to the elite Spanish financial society and took him to the brink of a political career.

He spent heavily on modernising the bank and reorganised its industrial interests in a holding company. But panic in world markets over the 1990 Gulf conflict foiled plans to float the holding company's shares and a steep recession brought losses in many of its industrial interests.
Unlike colleagues at other banks, Conde began aggressively attracting deposits and expanding Banesto's loan portfolio but in 1993 a recession in Spain was clearly hurting the bank.

The state bailout cost 192 billion pesetas ($1.7 billion). A parliamentary committee investigating the bank's collapse said it was due partly to Conde's aggressive campaign to build up Banesto's loan portfolio just as a recession set in.
The committee found the level of bad debts had been concealed from shareholders and auditors.
